content.title: About
content.content: Beef steak NFS is a premium cut taken from the loin of the cow. It is known for its tender flavor, juiciness, and characteristic marbling, making it perfect for grilling, pan‑searing or roasting.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NFS (No Fat Separation) indicates minimal fat loss during cooking.
Beef steak is one of the richest sources of iron and zinc.
Meat quality depends heavily on cattle breed, rearing conditions and aging process.
Traditionally the steak is cooked to medium‑rare to preserve maximum flavor and moisture.
Beef contains all essential amino acids required by the human body.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef steak provides complete protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef is highly bioavailable and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function, wound healing and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Creatine and carnitine
items.content: These compounds boost muscular energy and aid recovery after intense exercise.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive consumption of red meat may raise cholesterol levels and increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens such as E. coli; cook to a safe internal temperature.

items.title: Allergy or sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef, especially if they have a food allergy.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large portions of red meat can cause heaviness, indigestion or constipation in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The steak is best cooked over high heat—grill, pan‑sear or roast to the desired doneness. Let the meat rest at room temperature for 20‑30 minutes before cooking. Serve with vegetables, sauces, or simply season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the steak refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed bag; it will keep up to 6 months. Thaw frozen steak in the refrigerator before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Angel food cake is a light, airy dessert made from egg whites, sugar, and flour. It has a delicate flavor and virtually no fat, making it a popular choice for low‑calorie desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the cake’s fluffy, “angelic” texture.
Traditionally it is made without yolks, which gives it a more porous crumb.
In the United States it is often used as a base for fruit tarts and mousses.
A cream‑of‑tartar or acid is added to stabilize egg whites and achieve maximum rise.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Because only egg whites are used, the cake contains very little saturated fat, which is heart‑friendly.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Egg whites provide a complete source of protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Moderate glycemic impact
items.content: When consumed in reasonable portions, angel food cake raises blood sugar more gently than richer, butter‑laden cakes.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: The cake contains egg whites, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Typical recipes use a fair amount of sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Fragile texture
items.content: Angel food cake is delicate and can crumble easily, so it should be sliced and handled gently.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake with berry coulis, fresh fruit, a light whipped topping, or simply dusted with powdered sugar. It is also commonly used as a layer in multi‑tiered desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the finished cake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee is a beverage made from roasted and ground seeds of the coffee plant. There are two main types: instant (soluble) and brewed. Decaffeinated (decaf) coffee undergoes a special process to remove most of the caffeine while preserving flavor and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coffee is the second most traded commodity in the world after oil.
The first coffee beans were discovered in Ethiopia and later spread throughout the Arab world.
More than 100 species of coffee trees exist, but commercial production focuses on Coffea arabica and Coffea robusta.
Instant coffee was invented in the early 20th century and quickly gained popularity due to its convenience.
Decaf can be produced by the Swiss water process, which uses no chemical solvents.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and may reduce the risk of certain diseases.

items.title: Boosts mental alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving concentration and reaction time.

items.title: Supports metabolism
items.content: Caffeine can increase metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: May lower risk of type 2 diabetes
items.content: Studies show that moderate regular coffee consumption is associated with a reduced incidence of diabetes.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee provides niacin, riboflavin, and pyridoxine, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after coffee consumption.

items.title: Increased stomach acidity
items.content: Coffee can stimulate gastric acid production, which may be problematic for gastritis or ulcer patients.

items.title: Impact on bone health
items.content: High caffeine intake can increase calcium excretion, so people at risk of osteoporosis should limit consumption.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of certain medications, such as antidepressants and stimulants.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Brewed coffee is prepared by pouring hot water over ground beans (French press, espresso, drip). Instant coffee is simply mixed with hot water. Decaf is available in both forms and is suitable for those who want to avoid caffeine while keeping the coffee flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Ground coffee loses aroma faster, so keep it refrigerated and use within a few weeks. Instant coffee should be kept dry and used before the best‑by date on the package.

content.title: About
content.content: Fennel is a perennial herb of the Apiaceae family cultivated for its edible bulb. Raw fennel bulb is crisp, mildly sweet with a hint of anise, and is used in salads, pickles, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bulb is rich in aromatic compounds, especially anethole, which gives it its distinctive scent.
Ancient Romans used fennel as a remedy for digestive complaints.
While fennel seeds are widely known, the bulb remains a regional specialty in Mediterranean cuisine.
Commercial varieties are selected for compact bulbs rather than plant height, which can reach up to 1.5 m.
In some cultures fennel symbolizes purity and appears in festive dishes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: The bulb provides vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Flavonoids and phenolic compounds in fennel protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Anethole stimulates bile production, aiding the digestion of fats.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fennel, ranging from skin rash to swelling.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Fennel can enhance the effects of anticoagulants, so caution is advised for people on blood thinners.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Large amounts of fennel may affect thyroid function due to its goitrogenic compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw fennel bulb is thinly sliced and added to salads, pickles, or used as a crunchy garnish for fish and meat dishes. It can also be lightly sautéed or roasted to soften the flavor while retaining its aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fennel in the refrigerator, wrapped in a damp towel or placed in a perforated bag. It stays fresh for up to two weeks. Remove wilted leaves and discard any parts that show signs of rot.

content.title: About
content.content: Liver paste (or pâté) is a ready‑to‑eat product made from finely ground animal liver (commonly beef, pork or poultry), seasoned with salt, spices and often enriched with butter, cream or vegetables. It is usually served cold as a spread on bread, crackers or used as a filling for sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Liver pâtés have been prepared since ancient Rome, where they were served as a “pastilla” of liver and spices.
Traditional French “pâté de campagne” often combines liver, meat, fat and aromatic herbs.
In many countries, such as Russia, liver pâté is a classic holiday dish.
Liver pastes can be sold ready‑to‑eat or require a brief bake in the oven before serving.
Vegetarian pâtés replace liver with legumes, nuts and mushrooms while mimicking the texture.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Liver provides high levels of heme iron, which is readily absorbed and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A from liver supports vision, immune function and skin health.

items.title: High in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Protein‑dense
items.content: Liver pâté supplies high‑quality animal protein important for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate (vitamin B9) aids cell division and is especially beneficial for pregnant women.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Liver is rich in cholesterol, so people with elevated cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Risk of toxin accumulation
items.content: Liver can accumulate toxins and heavy metals; choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Liver allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to liver products.

items.title: Excess vitamin A
items.content: Overconsumption of liver can lead to hypervitaminosis A, especially in children and pregnant women.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Liver paste is convenient to spread on bread, toast, crackers or use as a topping for canapés. It can also be mixed into salads, used to stuff vegetables, or incorporated into sauces. Serve it chilled or gently warmed, and keep it refrigerated.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store liver pâté in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 5‑7 days. For longer keeping, freeze it in a tightly sealed package for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet pickled peppers are whole or sliced sweet bell peppers that have been cured in a brine of vinegar, salt, spices, and sometimes sugar. The peppers retain a crisp texture while acquiring a tangy‑sweet flavor typical of traditional pickles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet bell peppers are very high in vitamin C – one medium pepper provides over 100 % of the daily requirement.
Pickling can preserve peppers for up to a year when stored properly.
Traditional recipes often include coriander, mustard seeds, garlic, and bay leaf for extra aroma.
Sweet pickled peppers are popular in Mediterranean, Asian, and Latin American cuisines.
They are used in salads, sandwiches, pizza, and as a garnish for meat dishes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and polyphenols in peppers help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A cup of pickled peppers contains about 30 kcal, making it a diet‑friendly snack.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in peppers promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled foods can be high in salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Pepper allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to capsaicin or other pepper components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The vinegar’s acidity may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet pickled peppers can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, pasta, pizza, omelets, or used as a garnish for meat and fish. Before serving, they are often drained of excess brine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the opened jar in the refrigerator with the lid tightly sealed. Properly stored, the product remains good for 3‑6 months. Discard any peppers that show mold, off‑smells, or discoloration.

rice-with-stewed-beans-puerto-rican-styl.title: Rice with Stewed Beans, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: The traditional Puerto Rican dish “arroz con gandules” is a fragrant rice cooked together with stewed beans (usually red kidney beans), spices, tomato sauce, and sometimes pork or sausage pieces. It delivers a rich, mildly spicy flavor and the distinctive aroma of Caribbean herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish dates back to the colonial era when Spanish settlers introduced rice and beans, which locals adapted to Caribbean tastes.
Stewed beans in Puerto Rico are often called “gandules,” from the Spanish word for pigeon peas.
Traditionally the rice is cooked in a tight‑fitting pot so it absorbs the bean broth and spices.
Many versions start with a “sofrito” – a blend of onion, garlic, sweet pepper, cilantro, and tomatoes sautéed in olive oil.
It is a staple at the San Juan Festival and a common everyday comfort food.

items.title: Rich source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides sustained energy release, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: High plant‑based protein
items.content: Beans add a substantial amount of protein, supporting muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Fiber and digestive support
items.content: Beans contribute dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Together rice and beans supply thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: iron and magnesium
items.content: Beans are a good source of iron, while rice provides magnesium, both important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If prepared with soy sauce or pre‑made seasoning mixes, the dish can become high in sodium.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Raw beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; they should be fully cooked.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve hot, garnished with fresh cilantro or chopped green onions. It pairs well with fried plantains, avocado slices, mango salsa, or a simple green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat on the stovetop or in a microwave, adding a splash of water to restore moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy chips are crunchy snacks made from whole soybeans that are roasted or baked until golden. They have a mild nutty flavor and are often seasoned with salt, spices, or soy sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy chips contain more protein than most traditional potato chips.
The production uses whole soy protein and is gluten‑free.
Soybeans are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown by humans for over 5,000 years.
Baked versions are less fatty than deep‑fried chips.
A wide range of flavors exists: barbecue, spicy chili, sea salt, and more.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A single serving of soy chips provides about 15 % of the daily recommended protein, beneficial for vegetarians and athletes.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Soy isoflavones have antioxidant properties and may support hormonal balance.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with conventional chips, soy chips contain mainly polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Soybeans are a good source of vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy, ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salted varieties can be high in sodium, which is a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Phytates
items.content: Soybeans contain phytates that may reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

items.title: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs)
items.content: Most soy crops are GMO; those avoiding GMOs should look for certified non‑GMO products.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soy chips are convenient as a standalone snack, tossed into salads, soups, or used as a crunchy topping for Asian‑style dishes. Choose versions without artificial flavorings for a cleaner snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store soy chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 2–3 weeks to maintain crispness and flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: White wine is made from white or light‑colored grapes, and also from dark varieties that are pressed without skins. It displays a pale golden to light‑green hue and a characteristic fruity aroma with notes of citrus, apple, pear, and sometimes tropical fruits. The taste is usually light, refreshing, with moderate acidity and a soft tannic structure.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest references to white wine date back to ancient Rome, where it was prized for its lightness and ability to quench thirst in hot weather.
The most famous white wine grape is Chardonnay, cultivated in more than 70 countries worldwide.
Sauvignon Blanc wines often exhibit distinctive green pepper and herbaceous notes.
Traditional "méthode champenoise" (secondary fermentation in the bottle) is used not only for sparkling wines but also for some white wines, giving them a fine mousse.
White wine is frequently used in cooking for sauces, marinades, and desserts because its acidity enhances flavors.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds and resveratrol in white wine help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: May modestly reduce cardiovascular risk
items.content: Moderate intake (150‑200 ml per day) can improve lipid profiles and raise HDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Mild acidity stimulates gastric juice production, aiding the digestion of meals.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: White wines, especially those from fresh grapes, contain thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin.

items.title: Mild diuretic effect
items.content: Water and a small amount of alcohol promote the elimination of excess fluids.

items.title: Alcohol effects
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to dependence, liver damage, and other health issues.

items.title: Sulfite allergy
items.content: Sulfites used as preservatives may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain medications, including anticoagulants and diabetes drugs.

items.title: Caloric content
items.content: White wine contains about 80 kcal per 100 ml, so it should be accounted for in daily energy balance.

items.title: Not recommended for pregnant women
items.content: Alcohol may adversely affect fetal development; pregnant women should abstain completely.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve white wine chilled (8‑12 °C) in narrow‑rimmed glasses to concentrate the aroma. It pairs well with seafood, light salads, chicken in creamy sauces, and soft cheeses. In cooking, use it in sauces, marinades, and desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bottle in a cool, dark place, stored horizontally so the cork stays moist. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days, sealing tightly and refrigerating.

content.title: About
content.content: Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting grape juice, with red, white, rosé, and sparkling styles. It has been made for thousands of years and is enjoyed with meals and at celebrations and used in cooking. Wine contains alcohol, and health organizations do not recommend drinking alcohol for health benefits. It is intended only for adults of legal drinking age who choose to drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wine is made by fermenting grape juice, in which yeast converts the grape sugar into alcohol.
Red wine is fermented with the grape skins, which gives it its color and tannins, while white wine is usually made from juice without skins.
Wine has been made for at least 6,000 to 8,000 years in the South Caucasus region and elsewhere.
The flavor of wine depends on the grape variety, climate, soil, and winemaking.
Wine is also used in cooking, in sauces and braises, though some alcohol can remain in the dish.

items.title: Contains grape polyphenols
items.content: Red wine contains polyphenols such as resveratrol and anthocyanins from grape skins, though eating grapes or drinking grape juice provides these without alcohol.

items.title: Provides small amounts of minerals
items.content: Wine contains small amounts of potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Culinary use
items.content: Wine adds depth to sauces, stews, and marinades.

items.title: Cultural and social role
items.content: Wine is part of meals and celebrations in many cultures.

items.title: Limited health benefit
items.content: Any possible benefit of wine is small, and current evidence does not support drinking alcohol for health, since the risks of alcohol outweigh the possible benefits.

items.title: Alcohol and health
items.content: Alcohol is linked to liver disease, high blood pressure, certain cancers, accidents, and dependence, and no level of drinking is considered completely risk-free. If you do not drink, there is no health reason to start.

items.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.content: Alcohol should be avoided during pregnancy and while trying to conceive, and it is not recommended while breastfeeding.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol can interact with many medications, including sedatives, antidepressants, pain relievers, antibiotics, blood thinners, and diabetes medicines. Ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take any medication.

items.title: Dependence, driving, and sensitivities
items.content: Alcohol can be addictive and impairs judgment and driving, and sulfites or other compounds can cause headaches or reactions in some people. Wine is not for minors, people with liver disease, or people with a history of alcohol problems.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: If you are an adult and choose to drink, wine is usually served in small glasses with food, sipped slowly, and chilled according to its style. Alternate with water, avoid drinking on an empty stomach, and never drink and drive. In cooking, wine can flavor sauces and stews, although some alcohol remains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened wine on its side in a cool, dark place at a steady temperature, roughly 10 to 15 °C (50 to 59 °F). Once opened, recork it and refrigerate it. Still wine usually keeps for three to five days and sparkling wine for one to three days. Discard wine that smells like vinegar.
